title: IL-25 · Professional Certificate in Cybersecurity
tagline: Think like an attacker. Defend like a professional.
blurb: IL-25 is a 96-hour independent practice course aligned to the public topic map of a well-known 24-week professional cybersecurity certificate program. Across three phases — risk and governance foundations, defensive operations, and offensive security plus capstone — you build firewalls, triage logs, dissect phishing, audit cloud configurations, scope pentests, and close with a portfolio-grade capstone and a 120-minute mock circuit.
honestyNote: This is an independent preparation course aligned to the program's publicly described topic map; it is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or a substitute for MIT xPRO, confers no certificate, and grants no credential. All exposition is original practice material, and the assessments are for self-study only.
objectives: Assess organizational cyber risk using the threat-vulnerability-impact model and communicate findings in business terms.
Design layered defensive architectures spanning network, endpoint, identity, and data controls aligned to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework.
Execute incident response operations following the NIST SP 800-61 lifecycle, from detection through post-incident lessons learned.
Analyze adversarial techniques using MITRE ATT&CK and the cyber kill chain to build detections and prioritize defenses.
Evaluate cloud, OT/IoT, and AI systems for misconfigurations and emerging threats, applying appropriate guardrails.
Construct professional security deliverables — risk registers, pentest reports, and IR timelines — suitable for a hiring portfolio.

arc.title: Risk & Governance Foundations
arc.body: Modules 1-8 build the bedrock: risk management and the CIA triad, computing and networking foundations, federal law and standards (NIST CSF, RMF), threats and vulnerabilities, critical infrastructure, identity and access management, defensive operations concepts, and cryptography. You learn to speak risk, read the law and frameworks, and understand how systems are attacked and defended at a structural level.

arc.title: Defensive Operations
arc.body: Modules 9-16 put you in the defender's seat: SOC operations and SIEM-driven detection, incident response per NIST SP 800-61, secure system and network administration, cloud security and the shared responsibility model, then the adversary's view through offensive security concepts, social engineering, and AI security. Every module pairs theory with hands-on labs — firewall rules, log triage, header analysis, IAM audits.

arc.title: Offensive Security & Capstone
arc.body: Modules 17-24 complete the arc: penetration testing methodology with strict scoping and rules of engagement, policy/privacy/governance, OT/IoT security, and a capstone project where you run a full engagement lifecycle — threat model, defend, detect, respond, and report. You graduate with a portfolio artifact and a 120-minute mock circuit proving readiness.

modules.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity Risk Management
modules.summary: Risk management is the discipline of deciding which cyber risks are worth fighting, and how. This module teaches the core vocabulary — threat, vulnerability, impact, likelihood — and the assess-treat-monitor loop that turns vague fear into a prioritized plan. Independent study aligned to the MIT xPRO Professional Certificate in Cybersecurity topic map; not affiliated with MIT and confers no certificate.
objectives: Define threat, vulnerability, impact, likelihood, and residual risk in plain language.
Apply the risk equation (risk = threat × vulnerability × impact) to rank scenarios qualitatively.
Distinguish the four risk treatments: avoid, mitigate, transfer, and accept.
Build a basic risk register for a small organization or home lab.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Risk** — the potential for loss or harm when a threat exploits a vulnerability; commonly expressed as threat × vulnerability × impact.
- **Threat** — anything that could cause harm: a ransomware gang, a phishing email, a disgruntled employee, or a flood.
- **Vulnerability** — a weakness a threat can exploit: an unpatched server, a weak password policy, or an unlocked door.
- **Impact** — the damage if the event happens: money lost, downtime, reputational harm, legal penalties.
- **Likelihood** — how probable the event is, estimated from history, threat intelligence, and exposure.
- **Risk treatments** — avoid (stop the activity), mitigate (add controls), transfer (buy cyber insurance), accept (document and live with it).
- **Residual risk** — the risk left over after controls are applied; it is what leadership formally accepts.
- **Risk appetite** — how much risk an organization will take to achieve its goals; it guides every prioritization call.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Open a blank spreadsheet and create columns: Asset, Threat, Vulnerability, Likelihood (1–5), Impact (1–5), Risk score, Treatment, Owner.
1. List five assets you care about: your laptop, your email account, a family photo archive, your home router, and one work or school account.
2. For each asset, write one realistic threat and the vulnerability it would exploit (e.g., threat: credential-stuffing bots; vulnerability: password reuse).
3. Score likelihood and impact 1–5 and multiply for a risk score.
4. Sort by score and assign each row a treatment — avoid, mitigate, transfer, or accept — plus a named owner (you).
5. Take the top row and write one concrete mitigation you can finish this week, such as enabling MFA or applying updates.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Write a one-page risk assessment memo for a fictional 20-person accounting firm. Identify its five most important information assets, list two threats per asset with the vulnerabilities each exploits, and score likelihood × impact. Recommend one treatment per top-three risk with a rough cost estimate (free, cheap, expensive). Close with the residual risk statement the firm's owner would sign. Deliverable: a single PDF or markdown page, plain language, no unexplained jargon.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body: Pause and think like a risk owner, not a technician. Which of your own digital assets would hurt most to lose — and which treatment have you actually been applying to it: mitigation, or silent acceptance? Self-check: 1) What is the difference between a threat and a vulnerability? 2) Name the four risk treatments. 3) What is residual risk?

cards.back: The potential for loss when a threat exploits a vulnerability; often framed as threat × vulnerability × impact.
Any person, event, or condition that could cause harm — e.g., ransomware operators, phishing, insiders, natural disasters.
A weakness a threat can exploit — e.g., unpatched software, weak passwords, misconfigured services.
The damage if a risk materializes: financial loss, downtime, reputation harm, or legal penalties.
The estimated probability that a threat will exploit a vulnerability, based on exposure and history.
The risk remaining after controls are applied — the portion leadership formally accepts.
Shifting financial consequences to a third party, typically through cyber-insurance; it does not remove the risk itself.
The amount of risk an organization is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives; it guides prioritization.

quiz.q: In the standard risk equation, risk is best expressed as:
quiz.explain: The canonical formulation is risk = threat × vulnerability × impact, often simplified to likelihood × impact. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Buying cyber-insurance is an example of which risk treatment?
quiz.explain: Insurance transfers the financial consequence to a third party; the underlying risk still exists. (Concepts)

quiz.q: An unpatched web server is best described as a:
quiz.explain: The unpatched server is a weakness — a vulnerability — that a threat such as an attacker could exploit. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Risk that remains after security controls are applied is called:
quiz.explain: Residual risk is what is left over after mitigations; leadership formally accepts it. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Shutting down a risky legacy service entirely is an example of:
quiz.explain: Eliminating the activity removes the risk — that is avoidance. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Which of these is a threat rather than a vulnerability?
quiz.explain: A phishing campaign is an active source of harm (threat); the others are weaknesses (vulnerabilities). (Concepts)

quiz.q: A risk register is primarily used to:
choices: Track identified risks, scores, treatments, and owners
quiz.explain: A risk register documents each risk with its score, treatment, and owner so nothing is forgotten. (Hands-on procedure)

quiz.q: Qualitative risk assessment differs from quantitative mainly in that it:
choices: Uses descriptive ratings like high/medium/low instead of precise numbers
quiz.explain: Qualitative assessment uses descriptive scales (high/medium/low) while quantitative uses numbers and dollar values. (Concepts)

modules.title: Cybersecurity Foundation Concepts
modules.summary: Every security decision rests on a small set of foundation concepts — the CIA triad, defense in depth, least privilege, and zero trust. This module builds that shared vocabulary so later modules can move fast without re-explaining the basics. Independent study aligned to the MIT xPRO Professional Certificate in Cybersecurity topic map; not affiliated with MIT and confers no certificate.
objectives: Explain confidentiality, integrity, and availability, giving an example of each.
Describe defense in depth and least privilege and why they reduce breach impact.
Compare the three authentication factor types and explain multi-factor authentication.
Identify an organization's attack surface in a simple scenario.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Confidentiality** — information is accessible only to those authorized; enforced with encryption, access controls, and classification.
- **Integrity** — data is accurate and unaltered; protected with hashing, checksums, digital signatures, and change control.
- **Availability** — systems and data are reachable when needed; supported by redundancy, backups, and incident response.
- **Defense in depth** — layered controls (firewall, MFA, encryption, monitoring) so one failure does not equal total compromise.
- **Least privilege** — every user and process gets only the minimum access needed, shrinking the blast radius of compromise.
- **Zero trust** — “never trust, always verify”: verify every request, whatever the network location.
- **Attack surface** — the sum of all points where an attacker could get in: open ports, web apps, user accounts, APIs.
- **Authentication factors** — something you know (password), something you have (phone/token), something you are (fingerprint).

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run a personal security-basics audit.
1. List your ten most important online accounts (email, banking, school, work).
2. For each, record: does it use a unique password? Is MFA enabled? What factor type is the second factor?
3. Turn on MFA everywhere it is offered, preferring authenticator apps or passkeys over SMS.
4. Open your phone's app permissions and revoke location, camera, and contacts access from apps that do not need them — a least-privilege exercise.
5. Write a three-line summary: which account was your weakest link, and what did you change?

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Pick a familiar service (your bank's app, your school's portal, a streaming service) and write a CIA triad analysis: one paragraph each on how it protects confidentiality, integrity, and availability, citing observable features such as the login screen, password reset flow, or status page. Then list three ways its attack surface could be reduced. Deliverable: a one-page write-up in plain language.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body: Think about your own habits: where are you trading convenience for confidentiality? Pick one account and commit to one change this week. Self-check: 1) What does each letter of the CIA triad mean? 2) How does least privilege limit damage? 3) What are the three authentication factor types?

cards.back: Only authorized parties can access information; enforced via encryption and access controls.
Data remains accurate and unaltered; protected with hashes, signatures, and change control.
Systems and data are accessible when needed; supported by redundancy, backups, and response plans.
Layered security controls so a single failure does not lead to total compromise.
Granting users and processes only the minimum access required for their task.
“Never trust, always verify” — authenticate and authorize every request, even inside the network.
The total set of entry points an attacker could use: ports, apps, accounts, APIs.
Multi-factor authentication: requiring two or more factor types (know / have / are) to verify identity.

quiz.q: The “C” in the CIA triad stands for:
quiz.explain: Confidentiality — keeping information accessible only to authorized parties — is the C of the triad. (Concepts)

quiz.q: A file's hash no longer matches its recorded value. Which triad pillar is violated?
quiz.explain: A changed hash means the data was altered — an integrity failure. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Requiring a password plus an authenticator-app code is an example of:
quiz.explain: Two different factor types (know + have) make it multi-factor authentication. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Defense in depth means:
choices: Layering multiple controls so one failure is not fatal
quiz.explain: Layered controls ensure no single failure equals total compromise. (Concepts)

quiz.q: An intern's account can read the entire finance database. This violates:
quiz.explain: The account holds far more access than its role needs — a least-privilege violation. (Concepts)

quiz.q: “Never trust, always verify” is the motto of:
quiz.explain: Zero trust assumes no implicit trust based on network location. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Which pair are both authentication factors of the “something you have” type?
choices: Hardware token and smartphone authenticator app
quiz.explain: A hardware token and a phone app are both physical possessions — “something you have.” (Concepts)

quiz.q: Reducing open ports, disabling unused services, and removing stale accounts all:
quiz.explain: Fewer entry points means a smaller attack surface for attackers to probe. (Concepts)

modules.title: The Federal Government Role: Law, Operations, and Standards
modules.summary: Governments set the rules of the road for cybersecurity through law, operations, and voluntary standards. This module covers the U.S. federal role — key agencies, landmark laws, and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework — so you can speak the language of compliance. Independent study aligned to the MIT xPRO Professional Certificate in Cybersecurity topic map; not affiliated with MIT and confers no certificate.
objectives: Name the six NIST Cybersecurity Framework functions and what each covers.
Describe the roles of CISA and NIST in U.S. cybersecurity.
Explain what FISMA requires of federal agencies.
Map a sample control to the correct CSF function.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)** — a voluntary, widely adopted framework organized into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
- **Govern** — strategy, policy, and oversight: the organization's risk strategy and roles.
- **Identify** — know what you have: asset management, risk assessment, threat awareness.
- **Protect** — safeguards: access control, training, data security, hardening.
- **Detect** — monitoring and anomaly detection to catch events quickly.
- **Respond** — incident response planning, communications, and mitigation.
- **Recover** — restoring operations: backups, recovery planning, lessons learned.
- **FISMA** — requires federal agencies to implement information security protections and report on them.
- **CISA** — the federal operational lead for critical infrastructure protection and incident response coordination.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Do a mini CSF mapping exercise.
1. Pick an organization you know (a school, a small business, your home network).
2. Write down six real safeguards it already has — e.g., antivirus, backups, a firewall, password rules, software updates, an incident contact list.
3. Assign each safeguard to exactly one CSF function: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, or Recover.
4. Note which functions have zero safeguards — those are your gaps.
5. Draft one sentence per gap describing the cheapest realistic fix, and order the fixes by impact.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Write a two-page executive brief explaining the NIST CSF to a non-technical manager: what each of the six functions means, one example control per function, and why the framework is voluntary yet widely used. Include a simple table mapping five controls from your own environment to functions. Deliverable: a polished PDF or markdown document suitable for a board packet.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body: Compliance is a floor, not a ceiling — frameworks guide, but attackers don't read them. Ask yourself: which CSF function is weakest in your own setup? Self-check: 1) Name the six CSF functions in order. 2) What does FISMA require? 3) What is CISA's role?

cards.back: Voluntary cybersecurity framework organized into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
The CSF function covering strategy, policy, risk management, and oversight roles.
The CSF function covering asset management, risk assessment, and understanding threats.
The CSF function covering safeguards: access control, training, data security, hardening.
The CSF function covering continuous monitoring and anomaly detection.
The CSF function covering incident response planning, communication, and mitigation.
The CSF function covering restoration of operations, backups, and lessons learned.
U.S. law requiring federal agencies to implement information security protections and report on their programs.

quiz.q: How many functions make up the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0?
quiz.explain: CSF 2.0 has six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Continuous monitoring for anomalies belongs to which CSF function?
quiz.explain: Detect covers timely discovery of cybersecurity events through monitoring. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Restoring systems from backups after an incident maps to:
quiz.explain: Recover covers restoring operations and returning to normal after an incident. (Concepts)

quiz.q: FISMA applies primarily to:
quiz.explain: The Federal Information Security Modernization Act governs federal agency security programs. (Concepts)

quiz.q: CISA's primary mission is to:
choices: Protect critical infrastructure and coordinate incident response
quiz.explain: CISA is the federal operational lead for critical infrastructure protection and incident coordination. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Security awareness training for employees best fits which CSF function?
quiz.explain: Training is a safeguard that reduces human risk — squarely in Protect. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Which statement about the NIST CSF is most accurate?
choices: It is voluntary and widely adopted
It is mandatory for all U.S. businesses
quiz.explain: The CSF is a voluntary framework, yet it is widely adopted across sectors. (Concepts)

quiz.q: An incident response playbook belongs to which function?
quiz.explain: Playbooks for handling events are core to the Respond function. (Concepts)

modules.title: Threats and Vulnerabilities
modules.summary: Attackers have a playbook, and defenders must know it cold. This module surveys the threat landscape — malware families, social engineering, threat actor types — and how vulnerabilities are cataloged and found. Independent study aligned to the MIT xPRO Professional Certificate in Cybersecurity topic map; not affiliated with MIT and confers no certificate.
objectives: Classify common malware types: virus, worm, trojan, ransomware, spyware.
Explain how phishing and social engineering bypass technical controls.
Describe what a CVE entry provides and how it is used.
Compare vulnerability scanning with penetration testing.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Malware** — malicious software: viruses need a host and user action; worms self-propagate; trojans pose as legitimate apps.
- **Ransomware** — encrypts data and demands payment for the key; often paired with data theft (double extortion).
- **Spyware** — secretly monitors activity and steals keystrokes and credentials.
- **Phishing** — fake messages impersonating trusted senders to steal credentials or deliver malware; spear phishing targets specific people.
- **Social engineering** — manipulating people, not systems: pretexting, baiting, and tailgating exploit trust and urgency.
- **Threat actors** — from lone criminals to ransomware gangs, hacktivists, insiders, and APTs.
- **CVE** — Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: the public catalog assigning unique IDs and severity scores to known vulnerabilities.
- **Scanning vs. pen testing** — scanning automatically finds known weaknesses; pen testers actively attempt exploitation under defined rules.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Practice safe reconnaissance on your own network.
1. Install Nmap (or use your package manager) on a machine you own.
2. Scan only your home network: `nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24` (adjust to your subnet) to list live hosts — never scan networks you do not own or have permission to test.
3. Pick one of your own devices and run a basic port scan: `nmap <its IP>`.
4. For each open port, note the likely service and ask: does this need to be exposed?
5. Look up one CVE for a service you found and read what the entry discloses: affected versions, impact, and fix.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Write a threat briefing for a small business owner: profile three realistic threats (one malware, one phishing/social engineering, one insider), explain in plain language how each works, and recommend two practical defenses per threat. Include one CVE example relevant to software the business likely uses. Deliverable: a two-page briefing document.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body: The human is usually the weakest link — including you. When did you last click a link without thinking? Build the pause-and-verify habit. Self-check: 1) How does a worm differ from a virus? 2) What does ransomware do? 3) What is a CVE?

cards.back: Malware that attaches to a host file and needs user action to spread.
Self-propagating malware that spreads across networks without user action.
Malware disguised as legitimate software to trick users into installing it.
Malware that encrypts data and demands payment for the decryption key.
Fraudulent messages impersonating trusted senders to steal credentials or deliver malware.
Manipulating people — via trust, urgency, or deception — rather than attacking systems directly.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: the public catalog assigning unique IDs to known vulnerabilities.
Authorized, skilled testers actively attempting to exploit systems under defined rules of engagement.

quiz.q: Which malware type spreads across networks on its own, without user action?
quiz.explain: Worms self-propagate across networks; viruses need a host and user action. (Concepts)

quiz.q: “Double extortion” in ransomware means the attackers:
choices: Encrypt data and threaten to leak stolen copies
quiz.explain: Double extortion pairs encryption with the threat of publishing exfiltrated data. (Concepts)

quiz.q: A CVE identifier (e.g., CVE-2024-12345) primarily provides:
choices: A unique public reference for a known vulnerability
quiz.explain: CVE entries give each known vulnerability a unique ID, description, and severity data. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Spear phishing differs from bulk phishing in that it:
choices: Targets a specific person or organization with tailored lures
quiz.explain: Spear phishing tailors the lure to a specific target, unlike bulk campaigns. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Tailgating, as a security term, refers to:
choices: Following an authorized person through a secured door
quiz.explain: Tailgating is a physical social-engineering tactic: slipping in behind someone with legitimate access. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Vulnerability scanning differs from penetration testing mainly because scanning:
choices: Automatically checks for known weaknesses without attempting exploitation
quiz.explain: Scanners find known weaknesses automatically; pen testers actively attempt exploitation. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Which is the safest first step before running Nmap?
choices: Confirm you own the target network or have written permission
quiz.explain: Only scan systems you own or are authorized to test — unauthorized scanning can be unlawful. (Hands-on procedure)

quiz.q: An APT (advanced persistent threat) is best described as:
choices: A well-resourced, stealthy actor pursuing long-term access
quiz.explain: APTs are skilled, patient, well-resourced actors focused on sustained access. (Concepts)

modules.title: Cybersecurity for Critical Urban Infrastructure
modules.summary: Power grids, water systems, hospitals, and transit keep cities alive — and they are prime cyber targets. This module examines how operational technology differs from IT, why critical infrastructure is uniquely hard to defend, and how resilience is built. Independent study aligned to the MIT xPRO Professional Certificate in Cybersecurity topic map; not affiliated with MIT and confers no certificate.
objectives: Explain how operational technology (OT) differs from traditional IT.
Describe what SCADA and industrial control systems do.
Name several of the sixteen U.S. critical infrastructure sectors.
Analyze why patching and downtime work differently in OT environments.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Critical infrastructure** — systems vital to national life: energy, water, healthcare, transport, finance. The U.S. designates sixteen sectors.
- **OT** — operational technology: hardware and software controlling physical processes like pumps, turbines, and factory robots.
- **IT vs. OT** — IT guards data confidentiality; OT guards the safety and availability of physical processes, often on aging gear.
- **SCADA** — Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition: operators monitor and control industrial processes through sensor data.
- **ICS** — industrial control systems: SCADA plus programmable logic controllers (PLCs).
- **IT/OT convergence** — linking control networks to business networks and the internet: efficient, but it exposes OT to IT-style attacks.
- **Resilience** — keeping essential services running, or restoring them fast, during and after an incident.
- **Safety instrumented systems** — last-resort safeguards that shut a process down safely when controls fail.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Run a tabletop exercise for a fictional city water utility.
1. Write a one-paragraph scenario: ransomware has encrypted the billing network and is probing the SCADA network.
2. List the first five decisions the response team must make in the first hour (isolate networks? shut pumps? notify whom?).
3. Identify which OT constraints change the answer versus a normal IT incident (can you reboot a chlorination controller? can you patch it today?).
4. Draft the public statement the mayor's office would release, balancing honesty with avoiding panic.
5. Write three lessons-learned actions that would have reduced the impact.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Choose one critical infrastructure sector (energy, water, healthcare, or transportation) and write a three-page sector risk profile: what the sector's OT looks like, its two most plausible cyber threat scenarios, why standard IT defenses fall short, and three resilience recommendations. Cite only public, well-established facts. Deliverable: a structured report.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body: Infrastructure attacks hit real people — no water, no power, no hospitals. That weight is why OT defenders prioritize safety over convenience. Self-check: 1) How does OT differ from IT in priorities? 2) What does SCADA stand for? 3) Why is patching harder in OT?

cards.back: Systems and assets vital to national life, such as energy, water, healthcare, and transportation.
Operational technology: systems that monitor and control physical processes like pumps and turbines.
Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition: systems collecting sensor data and controlling industrial processes.
Programmable logic controller: a rugged computer that automates a specific industrial process.
Connecting control networks to business networks and the internet — efficient, but it exposes OT to cyberattacks.
The ability to maintain or quickly restore essential services during and after an incident.
Physical isolation of a network from all others; increasingly rare and often bridged in practice.
The number of U.S. critical infrastructure sectors designated for federal protection efforts.

quiz.q: In OT environments, the top priority is typically:
choices: Safety and availability of physical processes
quiz.explain: OT protects physical processes where failure can injure people — safety and availability come first. (Concepts)

quiz.q: SCADA systems are primarily used to:
choices: Monitor and control industrial processes via sensor data
quiz.explain: SCADA gathers sensor data and enables control of industrial processes. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Why is patching often harder in OT than in IT?
choices: Reboots can halt physical processes and legacy devices may not tolerate updates
quiz.explain: OT devices run continuous physical processes on aging hardware, so patching risks downtime or breakage. (Concepts)

quiz.q: How many critical infrastructure sectors does the U.S. designate?
quiz.explain: The U.S. designates sixteen critical infrastructure sectors. (Concepts)

quiz.q: IT/OT convergence increases risk mainly because:
choices: It exposes control systems to internet-style attacks
quiz.explain: Connecting OT to business networks and the internet opens control systems to IT-style threats. (Concepts)

quiz.q: A PLC is best described as:
choices: A rugged computer that automates a specific industrial process
quiz.explain: Programmable logic controllers directly automate industrial equipment. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the sixteen U.S. critical infrastructure sectors?
quiz.explain: Energy, water, and healthcare are designated sectors; professional sports leagues are not. (Concepts)

quiz.q: The main goal of a tabletop exercise is to:
choices: Practice incident decision-making through a discussed scenario
quiz.explain: Tabletops walk responders through a scenario to rehearse decisions without real-world consequences. (Hands-on procedure)

modules.title: Identity and Access Management (IAM) Concepts
modules.summary: Identity is the new perimeter: most breaches start with a stolen or misused credential. This module covers authentication, authorization, and the account lifecycle — the IAM concepts behind every login screen you will ever defend. Independent study aligned to the MIT xPRO Professional Certificate in Cybersecurity topic map; not affiliated with MIT and confers no certificate.
objectives: Distinguish authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA).
Compare RBAC and ABAC access models.
Explain SSO, MFA, and passkeys and when each fits.
Describe the joiner-mover-leaver account lifecycle.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **AAA** — authentication proves who you are; authorization sets what you may do; accounting logs what you did.
- **MFA** — multi-factor authentication combines two or more factor types, blocking most credential attacks even when passwords leak.
- **Passkeys** — phishing-resistant, public-key credentials that replace passwords with device-bound key pairs.
- **SSO** — single sign-on: one login grants access to many apps, cutting password sprawl (but the identity provider becomes a prime target).
- **RBAC** — role-based access control: permissions attach to roles, and users inherit their role's permissions.
- **ABAC** — attribute-based access control: decisions weigh attributes like department, clearance, or time of day.
- **Least privilege** — accounts, especially privileged ones, hold only the access their role requires, reviewed regularly.
- **Joiner-mover-leaver** — the account lifecycle: provision on hire, adjust on role change, deprovision on departure.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Audit your own identity footprint.
1. Open your email account's security page and list every active session and connected third-party app.
2. Revoke sessions and app permissions you do not recognize or no longer use.
3. Enable MFA on the account using an authenticator app or passkey if supported.
4. Check whether your password appears in known breach data using a reputable breach-check service, and change it if exposed.
5. Write down your personal “leaver checklist”: the accounts you would lock down first if a device were stolen.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Design an IAM policy for a fictional 50-person company: define five roles with their permissions (RBAC), list which systems require MFA, state the password/passkey standard, and write the joiner-mover-leaver procedure with owners and timeframes (e.g., deprovision within 24 hours). Deliverable: a two-page policy document.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body: You are the perimeter now — your credentials are the keys to your kingdom. Treat them that way. Self-check: 1) What is the difference between authentication and authorization? 2) How does RBAC differ from ABAC? 3) What happens in the “leaver” step?

cards.back: Proving identity — e.g., logging in with a password, token, or biometric.
Determining what an authenticated identity is allowed to do.
Logging user actions for audit and accountability — the third A in AAA.
Role-based access control: permissions attach to roles, and users inherit their role's permissions.
Attribute-based access control: access decisions evaluate attributes like department, time, or device.
Single sign-on: one authentication event grants access to multiple applications.
A phishing-resistant, public-key-based credential that replaces passwords with device-bound key pairs.
Elevated permissions (e.g., administrator) that demand extra protection and regular review.

quiz.q: Verifying a user's identity at login is:
quiz.explain: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do. (Concepts)

quiz.q: In RBAC, permissions are assigned to:
quiz.explain: RBAC attaches permissions to roles; users get permissions through role membership. (Concepts)

quiz.q: ABAC makes access decisions based on:
choices: Attributes such as department, clearance, time, or device
quiz.explain: Attribute-based access control evaluates multiple attributes for fine-grained decisions. (Concepts)

quiz.q: SSO's main usability benefit is:
choices: One login granting access to many applications
quiz.explain: Single sign-on reduces password sprawl with one authentication event for many apps. (Concepts)

quiz.q: A passkey resists phishing because it:
choices: Uses public-key cryptography bound to the legitimate site and device
quiz.explain: Passkeys cryptographically bind to the real site, so fake login pages cannot capture them. (Concepts)

quiz.q: The “leaver” step of the account lifecycle requires:
choices: Promptly deprovisioning access when someone departs
quiz.explain: Deprovisioning on departure prevents orphaned accounts from becoming attack paths. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Which account type demands the strongest protection and most frequent review?
quiz.explain: Privileged accounts hold elevated access, making them prime targets requiring extra controls. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Logging which files a user opened, for later audit, is the AAA component called:
quiz.explain: Accounting records user actions to support audit and accountability. (Concepts)

modules.title: IAM Layers and Technology
modules.summary: Identity is the control plane of modern security: every access decision starts with knowing who or what is asking. This module walks the four IAM layers — identification, authentication, authorization, and accountability — and shows how MFA, role-based access, and federated identity implement them in real systems.
objectives: Explain the four IAM layers and the order in which they produce an access decision
Compare authentication factors and justify when multi-factor authentication is required
Contrast RBAC and ABAC and apply least privilege when designing access policy
Describe how SAML, OAuth 2.0, and OpenID Connect enable federated identity

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Identification** — the claim of who you are: a username, an account ID, a certificate subject. A claim alone carries no trust.
- **Authentication** — proving the claim with factors: something you know (password), something you have (hardware key), something you are (biometric). MFA requires two or more *different* factors; two passwords is not MFA.
- **Authorization** — what the proven identity may do. RBAC grants permissions through roles; ABAC evaluates attributes (department, device health, time). Both follow least privilege: only what the task needs.
- **Accountability** — binding actions to identities through logs so every grant, denial, and elevation is auditable.
- **Federation** — one identity provider vouches for users across services: SAML for enterprise SSO, OAuth 2.0 for delegated authorization, OpenID Connect for identity on top of OAuth.
- **Privileged access** — admin accounts get vaulted credentials, just-in-time elevation, and recorded sessions.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: On a Linux lab VM, build a miniature RBAC system. 1) Create two users (analyst1, analyst2) and a group (soc). 2) Create /srv/cases owned by root:soc with mode 2770 and confirm analyst1 can write while an outsider cannot. 3) Add analyst1 to sudo with a single allowed command via visudo (e.g. systemctl restart). 4) Log in as each user and record which actions succeed and which are denied. 5) Write a one-paragraph mapping: which layer (identification, authentication, authorization, accountability) did each step exercise, and where would MFA slot in?

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Write a two-page IAM policy for a fictional 50-person company. Include: a joiner/mover/leaver workflow (who provisions, who approves, who revokes, and within what SLA); an MFA rollout plan naming which roles require it on day one; a role matrix mapping three job functions to systems and permission levels under least privilege; and a quarterly access-review process with an owner. Deliverable: the policy document plus your role matrix as a table. Keep every control tied to one of the four IAM layers.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body: Pause and reflect: where have you personally seen identification confused with authentication (a username treated as proof)? Self-check: 1) Name the four IAM layers in order. 2) Why is a password plus a security question not MFA? 3) Give one example each of RBAC and ABAC from a workplace you know.

cards.back: The claim of identity (username, account ID). Makes no trust assertion on its own.
Proving an identity claim using one or more factors: know, have, or are.
Something you know (password), something you have (hardware key), something you are (biometric).
Authentication using two or more *different* factor categories, e.g. password plus hardware key.
Role-based access control: permissions are assigned to roles, and users are assigned to roles.
Attribute-based access control: access decisions evaluate attributes of user, resource, and context.
Granting only the minimum access needed to perform a task, nothing more.

cards.front: SAML vs OAuth 2.0 vs OpenID Connect
cards.back: SAML: enterprise SSO assertions. OAuth 2.0: delegated authorization without password sharing. OIDC: identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0.

quiz.q: Which sequence correctly orders the IAM layers as an access decision unfolds?
quiz.explain: You claim an identity, prove it, get authorized, and your actions are logged — in that order. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Which of these qualifies as multi-factor authentication?
choices: A password plus a password-reset security question
A password plus a fingerprint scan
Two different passwords entered in sequence
quiz.explain: MFA needs two or more distinct factor categories: know (password) plus are (fingerprint). (Concepts)

quiz.q: A policy grants database access based on department, device compliance state, and time of day. This is:
quiz.explain: Decisions driven by attributes of user, resource, and context are attribute-based access control. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Under least privilege, a help-desk analyst who occasionally reads logs should receive:
choices: Domain admin rights in case they are needed later
The same permissions as a senior engineer for simplicity
No access at all, to eliminate risk
Read-only log access, with elevation only when a task requires it
quiz.explain: Least privilege grants the minimum needed for the task, with just-in-time elevation for exceptions. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Which protocol is designed for delegated authorization without sharing the user's password?
quiz.explain: OAuth 2.0 lets an app act with scoped permission while the password never leaves the identity provider. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Accountability in IAM is primarily achieved through:
choices: Logging that binds actions to identities
quiz.explain: Accountability means every action is attributable to an identity via audit logs. (Concepts)

quiz.q: An administrator's credentials are vaulted and checked out only for approved change windows with the session recorded. This is an example of:
quiz.explain: Vaulting, just-in-time checkout, and session recording are core privileged-access controls. (Concepts)

quiz.q: OpenID Connect (OIDC) relates to OAuth 2.0 as:
choices: A replacement that removes the need for tokens
An identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0
A directory protocol for account provisioning
quiz.explain: OIDC adds standardized identity (ID tokens) on top of OAuth 2.0's authorization framework. (Concepts)

modules.title: Preparing for a Job in Cybersecurity Risk Management
modules.summary: Risk management roles reward clear thinking and clear writing more than any single tool. This module maps the GRC and risk-analyst landscape, shows how to frame your existing experience for these roles, and walks the interview topics and portfolio artifacts that hiring managers actually look for.
objectives: Describe GRC and risk-analyst roles, their duties, and the skills employers screen for
Translate prior work experience into risk-management resume bullets using concrete outcomes
Explain core interview topics: risk as likelihood x impact, risk treatment options, control types
Produce portfolio artifacts (risk register, control-gap note) that demonstrate analyst thinking

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **The roles** — GRC analyst: maintains control frameworks, supports audits, tracks findings. Risk analyst: identifies, assesses, reports risks. Compliance analyst: maps operations to requirements. Read the duties, not just the title.
- **How risk is expressed** — risk = likelihood x impact. Treatments: mitigate (add controls), accept (document and own it), avoid (stop the activity), transfer (insurance, contracts).
- **Frameworks you will meet** — NIST Cybersecurity Framework and NIST Risk Management Framework; ISO 27001 for management systems; SOC 2 for service-provider trust. No certification needed to discuss them.
- **Resume framing** — translate past work: documenting procedures becomes 'control documentation'; spotting problems becomes 'risk identification'. Quantify honestly: systems covered, findings closed.
- **Interview currency** — walk through a risk assessment end to end, explain a control gap you found, and describe communicating a high risk to a non-technical manager.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: Build a mini risk register for a fictional small-business web store. 1) List 6 assets (customer database, payment page, admin laptop, backups, email, Wi-Fi). 2) For each, name one realistic threat and one vulnerability. 3) Score likelihood and impact 1-5 and multiply for an inherent risk score. 4) Propose one control per row, re-score residual risk, and pick a treatment (mitigate, accept, avoid, transfer). 5) Write a 3-sentence executive summary naming the top two risks and what you recommend. Use a spreadsheet; keep the math visible so an interviewer can follow it.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Assemble a one-page risk-analyst portfolio packet with three items: (1) your risk register from the lab, cleaned up and formatted; (2) a half-page control-gap analysis of a familiar system (home network, a school lab, a previous workplace) naming the framework control it maps to; (3) three rewritten resume bullets that translate your real experience into risk language with honest, verifiable outcomes. Deliverable: a single PDF. No invented employers, titles, or certifications — the packet must survive a background check.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body: Reflect: which of your past jobs already involved identifying or fixing risks, even if nobody called it that? Self-check: 1) State the four risk treatment options. 2) What is the difference between inherent and residual risk? 3) Name one control framework and what it is used for.

cards.back: Governance, Risk, and Compliance: the discipline of directing, assessing, and meeting security and regulatory obligations.
Risk = likelihood x impact. Scoring both lets you rank risks instead of treating them all equally.
Mitigate (add controls), accept (document and own the risk), avoid (stop the risky activity), transfer (insurance or contracts).
Inherent risk: before controls. Residual risk: what remains after controls are applied.
A voluntary framework organizing cybersecurity outcomes into functions like Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
International standard for an information security management system (ISMS), including a control annex.
An attestation report on a service provider's controls for security, availability, and related trust criteria.
A living document listing identified risks, scores, owners, treatments, and status.

quiz.q: A GRC analyst's core duties most likely include:
choices: Writing exploit code for penetration tests
Responding to live malware outbreaks on endpoints
Maintaining control documentation, supporting audits, and tracking findings
quiz.explain: GRC work centers on governance artifacts, audit support, and remediation tracking. (Concepts)

quiz.q: An analyst scores a risk likelihood 4 and impact 5. The risk score is:
quiz.explain: Risk = likelihood x impact, so 4 x 5 = 20. (Concepts)

quiz.q: A company buys cyber-insurance for a risk it cannot cheaply fix. This treatment is:
quiz.explain: Shifting financial consequence to an insurer is risk transfer. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Residual risk is best defined as:
choices: The risk before any controls are applied
A risk that has been transferred to insurance
Any risk scored below the reporting threshold
The risk that remains after controls are applied
quiz.explain: Residual risk is what is left over once controls do their work. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Which is the most honest way to frame help-desk experience for a risk-analyst resume?
choices: Claim a senior security title you never held
'Identified recurring access-request failures and documented a remediation checklist adopted by the team'
Invent an audit you did not perform
List a certification you plan to earn as already earned
quiz.explain: Translate real work into risk language with verifiable outcomes; never invent titles or credentials. (Concepts)

quiz.q: NIST CSF 2.0 organizes cybersecurity outcomes into functions including:
choices: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
quiz.explain: CSF 2.0's six functions are Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Discontinuing a risky legacy service rather than securing it is an example of:
quiz.explain: Stopping the activity entirely removes the risk — avoidance. (Concepts)

quiz.q: In an interview, the strongest way to discuss a past risk you handled is:
choices: Walk through identification, assessment, treatment, and the outcome in plain language
Recite framework clause numbers from memory
Claim the risk never existed to look competent
Blame the previous team for creating it
quiz.explain: A clear end-to-end walkthrough shows analyst thinking; jargon and blame do not. (Concepts)

modules.title: Introduction to Defensive Cybersecurity
modules.summary: Defense is about making attacks expensive and noisy, not impossible. This module introduces defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the layered controls — network, endpoint, and monitoring — that blue teams use to detect and blunt real attacks.
objectives: Apply the CIA triad to evaluate what a security control protects
Explain defense in depth and map controls to preventive, detective, and corrective types
Compare firewalls, IDS/IPS, and endpoint protection in a layered architecture
Use Nmap and Wireshark in a lab to observe what defenders see on the wire

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **CIA triad** — confidentiality (only authorized parties read it), integrity (not altered improperly), availability (reachable when needed). Every control serves at least one leg.
- **Defense in depth** — layered controls so one failure is not total failure: perimeter, network segmentation, endpoint, application, data, people.
- **Control types** — preventive (firewalls, MFA) blocks the event; detective (IDS, log monitoring) finds it; corrective (backups, reimaging) restores afterward.
- **Network defenses** — firewalls filter by rule; IDS alerts while IPS can block in line; segmentation (VLANs, subnets) limits lateral movement.
- **Endpoint and data** — EDR on hosts, patching to close known flaws, encryption at rest and in transit, tested backups for recovery.
- **Blue team mindset** — assume breach is possible, prioritize by risk, measure detection and response. MITRE ATT&CK gives defenders a shared map of adversary techniques.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: In an isolated lab network you own (two VMs or a home lab subnet), play defender. 1) From one VM, run an Nmap scan of the other and record open ports and services. 2) On the target, capture the scan with Wireshark and identify the probe packets. 3) Enable the host firewall, add a rule blocking one discovered service, and re-scan to confirm the port state changed. 4) Write up: which control type was each step (preventive, detective), which CIA leg it served, and what an IDS alert for this scan would look like. Never scan networks you do not own.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Design a defense-in-depth architecture for a fictional 30-person company with a public web app. Deliver a one-page network diagram (perimeter firewall, segmented subnets, endpoint protection, backup flow) plus a control table mapping at least 9 controls to their layer, control type (preventive/detective/corrective), and CIA leg. Add a short paragraph naming the single control you would fund first on a tight budget and why. Keep it realistic: no exotic products, just layered fundamentals.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body: Reflect: which layer of defense do you personally rely on most today (updates? backups? passwords?), and which is weakest? Self-check: 1) Define each leg of the CIA triad. 2) Is a backup preventive, detective, or corrective? 3) What is the difference between IDS and IPS?

cards.back: Only authorized parties can read the data.
Data is not altered improperly or without detection.
Authorized parties can access systems and data when needed.
Layered security controls so a single failure does not compromise everything.

cards.front: Preventive vs detective vs corrective control
cards.back: Preventive blocks the event; detective finds it; corrective restores afterward.
IDS (intrusion detection) watches and alerts; IPS (intrusion prevention) sits in line and can block.
Dividing a network into isolated segments (VLANs, subnets) to limit lateral movement.
The defensive side: detects, responds to, and recovers from attacks.

quiz.q: Encrypting customer records at rest primarily protects which leg of the CIA triad?
quiz.explain: Encryption keeps unauthorized parties from reading the data — confidentiality. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Defense in depth means:
choices: Buying the most expensive firewall available
Layering controls so one failure does not mean total compromise
Relying on a single strong perimeter
quiz.explain: Multiple independent layers absorb individual control failures. (Concepts)

quiz.q: A SIEM rule that pages an analyst when impossible-travel logins occur is a:
quiz.explain: It detects the event in progress rather than blocking or restoring. (Concepts)

quiz.q: The key operational difference between IDS and IPS is:
choices: IDS is hardware, IPS is software
IDS encrypts traffic; IPS decrypts it
IPS can block malicious traffic in line; IDS only detects and alerts
quiz.explain: An IPS sits in the traffic path and can drop packets; an IDS observes and raises alerts. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Segmenting the payment network from the office network mainly limits:
quiz.explain: Segmentation contains attackers to the segment they breached. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Tested offline backups are best classified as:
quiz.explain: Backups restore service after an incident — corrective, serving availability. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Patching a known vulnerability in a web server is:
quiz.explain: Patching removes the flaw before it can be exploited — prevention. (Concepts)

quiz.q: A defender studying MITRE ATT&CK is mainly gaining:
choices: A shared map of adversary tactics and techniques to align detections
A list of certified security products
quiz.explain: ATT&CK catalogs how adversaries operate so defenders can map coverage and gaps. (Concepts)

modules.title: Cryptography
modules.summary: Cryptography is the math that lets strangers trust each other over hostile networks. This module covers symmetric and asymmetric encryption, hashing, digital signatures, and PKI — what each one guarantees, what it does not, and where you meet them in everyday systems like TLS.
objectives: Distinguish symmetric from asymmetric encryption and choose the right one for a scenario
Explain what hashing guarantees and why it is not encryption
Describe how digital signatures provide authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation
Trace how PKI and certificates make TLS trust work in a browser session

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Symmetric encryption** — one shared secret key encrypts and decrypts (AES is the modern standard). Fast, suited to bulk data — but both sides must share the key securely first.
- **Asymmetric encryption** — key pair: public key encrypts, private key decrypts (RSA is the classic example). Solves key distribution but is slow, so it typically protects a symmetric session key.
- **Hashing** — a one-way function (SHA-256) producing a fixed-size digest. Not encryption: no key, no decryption. Used for integrity checks and password verifiers.
- **Digital signatures** — sign with the private key, verify with the public key: authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation.
- **Key exchange** — Diffie-Hellman lets two parties agree on a shared secret over a public channel, with no authentication by itself.
- **PKI and TLS** — certificate authorities vouch for public keys; browsers trust a preinstalled root list, which is what the padlock rests on.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: Use OpenSSL on a lab machine to touch every primitive. 1) Generate an RSA key pair and a self-signed certificate. 2) Encrypt a short text file with the public key, then decrypt with the private key. 3) Hash the file with SHA-256, change one byte, and hash again to see the digest change completely. 4) Sign the file with the private key and verify the signature with the public key, then tamper the file and watch verification fail. 5) Write two sentences for each step: what security property did you just demonstrate?

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Write a one-page encryption design brief for a fictional clinic's patient portal. Specify: what gets symmetric encryption (AES for data at rest and the TLS session), where asymmetric crypto appears (key exchange, certificate-based server authentication), what gets hashed (password verifiers with a salt, file integrity checks), and where digital signatures are used (software updates, audit logs). Add a 'what it does not protect' section — e.g., encryption does not stop phishing or a compromised endpoint. Deliverable: the brief as a PDF.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body: Reflect: where in your daily life do you rely on cryptography without noticing (banking apps, messaging, Wi-Fi)? Self-check: 1) Why is hashing not encryption? 2) What problem does asymmetric crypto solve that symmetric cannot? 3) What three properties does a digital signature provide?

cards.back: One shared secret key for both encryption and decryption. Fast; AES is the standard example.
Key pair: public key encrypts, private key decrypts. RSA is the classic example.
One-way function producing a fixed-size digest. No key, no decryption; used for integrity and password verifiers.
Sign with private key, verify with public key. Gives authentication, integrity, non-repudiation.
Protocol for two parties to agree on a shared secret over a public channel; no authentication alone.
Public key infrastructure: certificate authorities vouch for bindings between identities and public keys.
Trusted third party that issues digital certificates; browsers trust a preinstalled root list.
The signer cannot later deny having signed, because only their private key could have made the signature.

quiz.q: AES is best described as:
choices: A symmetric encryption algorithm used for bulk data
An asymmetric algorithm for digital signatures
A hashing function for password storage
quiz.explain: AES uses one shared key for encryption and decryption and is the standard for bulk symmetric encryption. (Concepts)

quiz.q: The main problem asymmetric encryption solves is:
choices: Making encryption faster for large files
Secure key distribution without a pre-shared secret
quiz.explain: Public/private key pairs let strangers communicate securely without first sharing a secret. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Which statement about hashing is TRUE?
choices: Hashing is encryption with a public key
A hash can be decrypted with the right key
Hashing is one-way: the digest cannot be reversed to the input
Two different inputs always produce the same digest
quiz.explain: Hash functions are one-way by design; there is no decryption step. (Concepts)

quiz.q: A software vendor signs its update package. A user verifying the signature gains:
choices: Proof of who published it, that it was not altered, and the vendor cannot deny it
quiz.explain: Signatures provide authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation. (Concepts)

quiz.q: In a typical TLS session, asymmetric cryptography is mainly used to:
choices: Encrypt the entire video stream for speed
Authenticate the server and protect the symmetric session key
quiz.explain: Asymmetric crypto handles authentication and key establishment; fast symmetric AES encrypts the bulk session. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Diffie-Hellman on its own does NOT provide:
choices: A shared secret over a public channel
A session key for symmetric encryption
quiz.explain: DH agrees on a secret but does not prove who you are talking to; pair it with authentication. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Storing passwords correctly means storing:
choices: The plaintext in an encrypted database column
An RSA-encrypted copy only the admin can read
The password split across two files
A salted hash (password verifier), never the password itself
quiz.explain: Salted hashes let you verify a login without ever storing a recoverable password. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Your browser trusts a website's certificate mainly because:
choices: The certificate chains to a root CA in the browser's trust store
The site paid for a domain name
quiz.explain: Trust comes from the CA chain terminating at a preinstalled trusted root, not from the URL text. (Concepts)

modules.title: Security Operations Center (SOC)
modules.summary: The SOC is where defense becomes a daily operation: alerts flow in, analysts triage them, and incidents get worked. This module covers SOC tiers and roles, the SIEM at the center of it, alert triage discipline, and the metrics that tell you whether the operation is actually working.
objectives: Describe SOC tier structure (L1/L2/L3) and what each tier owns
Explain the SIEM's role: aggregation, correlation, and alerting
Triage a security alert using a disciplined, evidence-first workflow
Interpret core SOC metrics: MTTD, MTTR, alert volume, and false-positive rate

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **SOC tiers** — L1 triages alerts: acknowledge, enrich, escalate or close. L2 investigates confirmed incidents: scope, contain, coordinate. L3 hunts proactively, tunes detections, handles threat intelligence.
- **SIEM** — aggregates logs across the estate, correlates events into alerts, and gives analysts one searchable timeline. Only as good as its log sources and tuned rules.
- **Alert triage** — verify before acting: check raw logs, enrich with context (asset criticality, user role), rule true vs false positive, escalate with evidence attached.
- **Runbooks and playbooks** — step-by-step procedures for common alert types (phishing, malware, impossible travel) so L1 responds consistently at 3 AM.
- **Metrics** — MTTD (mean time to detect), MTTR (mean time to respond/recover), alert volume per analyst, false-positive rate. A drowning L1 queue signals bad tuning or understaffing.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: Triage like an L1 analyst using sample data. 1) Take five mock alerts (impossible-travel login, malware hash match, port scan, failed logins x50, odd PowerShell). 2) For each, write: the raw evidence you would pull first, two enrichment questions (who owns the asset? is the user traveling?), and your disposition (true positive, false positive, benign, escalate). 3) Draft a three-line escalation note for the one you escalate to L2. 4) Finally, write one SIEM correlation rule in plain English that would have caught your true positive earlier. Time yourself: triage is a timed discipline.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Write a one-page SOC runbook for a 'suspected phishing with credential entry' alert. Include: trigger conditions, the first five evidence-gathering steps in order, decision points (when to escalate to L2, when to close as benign), containment actions L1 is authorized to take (disable account, block sender domain), and the documentation fields every ticket must carry. Add a short tuning note: what would you change if this alert fired 200 times a day with 95% false positives? Deliverable: the runbook as a PDF.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body: Reflect: triage is mostly deciding what NOT to panic about — where else in life do you already do that kind of filtering? Self-check: 1) What does each SOC tier own? 2) What is the first thing you do with a new alert? 3) What do MTTD and MTTR measure?

cards.back: First tier: triages alerts — acknowledge, enrich, escalate confirmed issues or close false positives.
Second tier: investigates confirmed incidents — scoping, containment, coordination.
Third tier: threat hunting, detection tuning, threat intelligence, complex cases.
Security information and event management: aggregates logs, correlates events, generates alerts, enables timeline search.
Disciplined workflow: verify raw evidence, enrich with context, disposition as true/false positive or escalate.
Documented step-by-step procedure for handling a specific alert or incident type consistently.
Mean time to detect: average time from compromise/activity start to detection.
Mean time to respond (or recover): average time from detection to containment/recovery.

quiz.q: An L1 analyst's primary job is to:
choices: Triage alerts: verify, enrich, escalate or close with evidence
quiz.explain: L1 owns the alert queue: quick verification and correct disposition or escalation. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Which task belongs to L3 rather than L1?
choices: Proactive threat hunting and detection tuning
quiz.explain: Hunting and tuning detections are senior proactive functions, not queue triage. (Concepts)

quiz.q: A SIEM's core value to a SOC is:
choices: Aggregating logs and correlating events into investigable alerts
quiz.explain: The SIEM centralizes log data and turns correlated events into alerts with searchable timelines. (Concepts)

quiz.q: The FIRST step in disciplined alert triage is:
choices: Email the whole company a warning
Check the raw log evidence before acting
Delete the alert to keep the queue clean
quiz.explain: Verify with raw evidence first; acting on an unverified alert causes damage and noise. (Concepts)

quiz.q: MTTD is rising quarter over quarter. This most directly signals:
choices: Analysts are closing tickets too fast
Detection is getting slower — review log sources and detection coverage
The SIEM license is too expensive
quiz.explain: Mean time to detect rising means threats dwell longer before discovery. (Concepts)

quiz.q: A runbook for 'impossible travel login' should include:
choices: Ordered evidence steps, decision points, authorized containment actions, documentation fields
Only the phone number of the CISO
Marketing copy for the security team
quiz.explain: Runbooks standardize response: steps, decisions, authorized actions, and required documentation. (Concepts)

quiz.q: An alert fires 500 times daily with a 98% false-positive rate. The right move is:
choices: Hire more L1 analysts to close them
Tune the detection rule to reduce noise while keeping true positives
quiz.explain: Alert fatigue kills a SOC; tuning the rule fixes the signal-to-noise ratio at the source. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Escalating from L1 to L2 should carry:
choices: A guess about the attacker's identity
The evidence gathered, enrichment context, and what was already ruled out
Nothing — L2 will figure it out
quiz.explain: Escalation moves evidence upward so L2 starts investigating, not re-triaging. (Concepts)

modules.title: Incident Response (IR)
modules.summary: When prevention fails, disciplined response limits the damage. This module teaches the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle — Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication, and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity — plus the evidence handling and communication habits that separate professionals from panickers.
objectives: Name and order the four NIST SP 800-61 incident response phases
Explain containment, eradication, and recovery as distinct steps with different goals
Describe evidence preservation and chain of custody during an incident
Run a tabletop exercise and write a lessons-learned report

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Phase 1: Preparation** — before anything happens: IR plan, defined roles, contact lists, tooling, trained staff, practiced playbooks. Not improvisable mid-incident.
- **Phase 2: Detection & Analysis** — validate the incident: confirm scope, determine what happened, prioritize by impact. Hasty conclusions cause wrong containment.
- **Phase 3: Containment, Eradication & Recovery** — containment stops the bleeding (isolate hosts, block indicators); eradication removes the cause (kill persistence, patch entry); recovery restores operations with heightened monitoring.
- **Phase 4: Post-Incident Activity** — lessons-learned review: timeline, what worked, what failed, improvements fed back into preparation.
- **Evidence handling** — preserve logs and images before remediation destroys them; keep chain of custody (who handled what, when).
- **Communication** — one spokesperson, need-to-know updates, prewritten templates.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body: Run a 45-minute tabletop exercise with a partner (or solo, writing both sides). Scenario: ransomware found on two finance workstations at 9 AM. 1) Preparation check: list the roles, contacts, and tools you would need — note what is missing. 2) Detection & Analysis: write the five questions you must answer before containing (patient zero? spread? data exfiltration?). 3) Containment/Eradication/Recovery: sequence your actions and justify the order. 4) Draft the internal notification for staff and the executive update. 5) Hold the lessons-learned: three things to improve. Keep the whole exercise to two pages.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Produce a two-page incident response plan for a fictional 40-person company plus a one-page lessons-learned template. The plan must cover: IR team roles and escalation contacts, the four NIST phases with entry/exit criteria for each, evidence-preservation steps, and communication rules (who speaks, who is told what, when legal is looped in). The template must capture timeline, root cause, impact, response effectiveness, and action items with owners. Deliverable: plan plus template as a single PDF.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body: Reflect: think of a past crisis (tech or otherwise) — what would a 'post-incident review' have caught that the moment itself missed? Self-check: 1) List the four NIST IR phases in order. 2) Why contain before eradicating? 3) What is chain of custody and why does it matter?

cards.back: Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Post-Incident Activity.
IR plan, roles, contacts, tools, training, and practiced playbooks — built before an incident.
Stopping the incident's spread (isolate hosts, block indicators) without destroying evidence.
Removing the root cause: kill persistence mechanisms, close the entry point, patch.
Restoring systems to normal operation with heightened monitoring for resurgence.
Documented record of who collected, handled, and stored evidence and when.
Post-incident analysis of timeline, effectiveness, and improvements fed back into preparation.
Discussion-based drill walking the IR team through a scenario without touching live systems.

quiz.q: The correct order of the NIST SP 800-61 phases is:
choices: Detection & Analysis; Preparation; Post-Incident Activity; Containment, Eradication & Recovery
Preparation; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Detection & Analysis; Post-Incident Activity
Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Post-Incident Activity
Containment, Eradication & Recovery; Preparation; Detection & Analysis; Post-Incident Activity
quiz.explain: NIST SP 800-61 orders them: prepare, detect/analyze, contain/eradicate/recover, then learn. (Concepts)

quiz.q: During Preparation, the most important deliverable is:
choices: A tested IR plan with defined roles, contacts, and playbooks
A list of hackers to blame
quiz.explain: Preparation means the plan, people, and practice exist before the incident starts. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Containment is performed BEFORE eradication mainly because:
choices: Stopping the spread first prevents further damage while you find the root cause
quiz.explain: You stop the bleeding before surgery: limit spread, then remove the cause. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Wiping and reimaging an infected host without first capturing logs and a disk image risks:
choices: Destroying evidence needed for root-cause analysis and chain of custody
quiz.explain: Remediation destroys evidence; preserve it first for analysis and potential legal needs. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Chain of custody matters because:
choices: It documents who handled evidence and when, preserving its credibility
It assigns blame to an employee
quiz.explain: Without a custody record, evidence may be inadmissible or untrustworthy. (Concepts)

quiz.q: The Post-Incident Activity phase exists to:
choices: Produce a lessons-learned review and feed improvements back into preparation
quiz.explain: Learning and improving is the phase's entire purpose; skipping it guarantees repeats. (Concepts)

quiz.q: In Detection & Analysis, the priority is to:
choices: Immediately shut down the whole network
Validate the incident, determine scope, and prioritize by impact
quiz.explain: Confirm what happened and how bad it is before choosing containment actions. (Concepts)

quiz.q: A tabletop exercise is valuable because it:
choices: Tests the IR plan and team coordination without risking live systems
Is required for all software licenses
quiz.explain: Discussion-based drills expose plan gaps cheaply and safely. (Concepts)

modules.title: Secure Systems Administration
modules.summary: Lock down the machines before attackers find them. This module covers operating-system hardening, least-privilege access, patch discipline, and the centralized logging you need to detect what slips through.
objectives: Apply OS hardening baselines (such as CIS Benchmarks) to remove unneeded services, accounts, and default credentials.
Implement least-privilege access with role separation and distinct privileged accounts for administrative work.
Build and operate a patch-management cycle: inventory assets, test updates, deploy on schedule, verify.
Configure centralized logging and key-based SSH so admin activity is auditable and remote access is phishing-resistant.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Hardening** — reducing a system’s attack surface by removing unneeded services, software, and accounts, then securing what remains.
- **Least privilege** — every user, process, and service receives only the permissions required for its job, nothing more.
- **CIS Benchmarks** — community-developed, vendor-neutral configuration baselines; a standard hardening starting point.
- **Patch management** — the cycle of inventorying assets, testing updates, deploying on schedule, and verifying; unpatched software is a top initial-access vector.
- **Secure baselines** — hardened images or configuration templates so every new host starts from a known-good state.
- **Account hygiene** — disable default accounts, enforce strong unique passwords plus MFA, and use separate privileged accounts for admin work.
- **Centralized logging** — forward authentication and privilege-escalation events to a collector; without logs you cannot detect or reconstruct incidents.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
1. On a lab Linux VM, update all packages and reboot.
2. List enabled services and disable anything non-essential.
3. Audit users: lock or remove unused accounts and verify there are no duplicate privileged UIDs.
4. Harden SSH: disable password authentication, require key-based login, and disable remote root login.
5. Enable the host firewall with a default-deny inbound policy, allowing only SSH from your management host.
6. From a second VM, run Nmap against the target and confirm only the expected port is open.
7. Document every change plus the before/after scan results in your lab notebook.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Produce a server-hardening report for a lab host. Start with a CIS-Benchmark-style checklist covering services, accounts, SSH, firewall, and logging. Record the pre-hardening state (open ports, enabled services, default accounts), apply your checklist, then record the post-hardening state with Nmap evidence. Deliver a 2–3 page report: checklist, before/after tables, residual risks, and a rollback note for each change.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body:
Reflection: which of your own devices would fail a CIS-style audit today, and what is the single highest-value fix?
Self-check:
1. What is the difference between hardening and patching?
2. Why should admin work use a separate privileged account?
3. Which three event types must reach your central log collector?

cards.back: Reducing a system's attack surface by removing unneeded services, software, and accounts, then configuring what remains securely.
The principle that every user, process, and service gets only the minimum permissions needed to do its job.
Community-developed, vendor-neutral secure configuration baselines for operating systems and applications.
Inventory assets, test updates, deploy on schedule, and verify — repeated continuously to close known vulnerabilities.
A hardened image or configuration template so every newly deployed host starts from a known-good state.
A firewall posture where all inbound traffic is blocked unless explicitly allowed by a rule.
Logging in with a cryptographic key pair instead of a password; resists brute-force and credential-phishing attacks.
Local logs can be altered or lost when a host is compromised; a central collector preserves evidence for detection and incident reconstruction.

quiz.q: The principle of least privilege states that:
choices: Users and services receive only the permissions they need to do their job
All users should share one administrator account for convenience
Permissions are granted permanently and never reviewed
Every account gets full local administrator rights
quiz.explain: Least privilege limits every identity to the minimum permissions required, which shrinks what an attacker gains from any single compromised account. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Which practice most directly reduces risk from unpatched software?
choices: Disabling all logging to save disk space
A documented patch-management cycle: inventory, test, deploy, verify
Sharing one admin password across the whole team
Opening firewall ports for vendor convenience
quiz.explain: A disciplined inventory-to-verification cycle is what actually closes known vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them. (Concepts)

quiz.q: CIS Benchmarks are best described as:
quiz.explain: CIS Benchmarks are consensus hardening guides, not products — they give administrators a vetted starting configuration. (Concepts)

quiz.q: Why should administrators use a separate privileged account instead of their daily-use account?
choices: It lets them use shorter passwords
It is required to play online games
It limits the damage if the daily-use account or workstation is compromised
quiz.explain: Separating privileged credentials means a compromise of the everyday account does not hand over administrator rights. (Concepts)

quiz.q: System hardening primarily aims to:
choices: Make the system boot faster for gaming
Reduce the attack surface by removing or securing unneeded services, accounts, and software
Install as many utilities as possible
Disable all security logging for performance
quiz.explain: Hardening is attack-surface reduction: less exposed software and fewer accounts means fewer paths in for an attacker. (Concepts)

quiz.q: In the hands-on procedure, after enabling a default-deny inbound firewall you verify the result by:
choices: Scanning the host with Nmap from a second VM and confirming only expected ports are open
Deleting the firewall rules you just created
Asking a friend to guess which ports are open
Disabling SSH entirely so nothing can connect
quiz.explain: An independent scan from another host proves the firewall behaves as configured instead of trusting the local config alone. (Hands-on procedure)

quiz.q: Which SSH hardening steps are applied in the lab?
choices: Enable Telnet as a backup access method
Allow root login with a short memorable password
Share one private key among the whole class
